newsitem.title: CANADA: Signs of hope appear in flood-ravaged Manitoba.
newsitem.headline: Signs of hope appear in flood-ravaged Manitoba.

text.p: As the Red River's levels remained stable and dikes held, Canadian emergency officials were optimistic on Monday that the worst may be over for flood-ravaged towns near the Manitoba-North Dakota border.
But upstream in the city of Winnipeg, flood preparations continued at a fever pitch as the swell of the Red moved slowly northward.

The level of silty brown water that surrounds the border town of Emerson, Manitoba, an evacuated farm community of 750, has held to within an inch (2.5 cm) over the past three days, giving officials hope the river had reached its peak there.

Brisk winds whipped up choppy waves on the huge lake that now covers the Red River Valley in rural southern Manitoba on Monday and officials feared that water crashing against barriers protecting communities would cause them to fail.

But Manitoba flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said government crews surveying the region by helicopter could see no evidence of major breaches in "ring" dikes around eight farming towns in the expanse of water.

"The people who are monitoring the situation in the valley communities are confident the dikes will hold," Whitney said. "The situation today with the heavy winds was going to be a test for us, but we seem to be coming through that just fine."

The Red River, which continued to swallow up vast tracts of rural land in the western Canadian province as the swell moved north, was estimated to be 18 miles (29 km) wide at the border with the United States.

About 17,000 people have been forced out from their homes in towns and on farms in the region. By Monday, more than 4,200 evacuees had registered at a Winnipeg sports arena for financial help and temporary refuge.

In Winnipeg, a city of 650,000 people, local officials concentrated on evacuating low-lying neighborhoods lining the river and making sure its southwest was protected from the quickly spreading lake. The Red is not projected to crest in the city until next Monday.

Winnipeg engineers feared a 25 mile (40 km) earthen wall, being hastily constructed by hundreds of workers and a phalanx of earth-moving machines to stop waters from a Red River tributary from spreading northward, could fail.
To prepare for that, Winnipeg crews began on Monday to reinforce a highway surrounding the city as a last line of defense for 10,000 people living in the city's southwest.
"Our job is to take every precaution to make sure there is a Plan B and a Plan C," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said.
In other parts of the city, residents place their faith in a huge ditch built in 1968 to divert high Red River waters around its limits.

At the sports arena-turned evacuee center in south Winnipeg on Monday, a stream of people forced from their southern Manitoba homes filed in to register with the Red Cross for flood relief and temporary living accommodations.
